segments.say: The rain on the glass slowly turns to something softer. You look up, and see that it's snowing now, large, slow flakes drifting down past the window, glowing in the light from the room. The attic has become a deep, cushioned window seat, in a stone cottage, and outside, the whole valley is white and silent.

The seat is wide enough to lie along, with a thick cushion beneath you and a heavy blanket on top. You curl into it, with your knees drawn up a little, your head on a soft pillow, facing the glass. There's a faint chill coming off the window, and the warm room behind you, and the contrast is deliciously cozy.

Outside, the snow falls in slow, silent spirals. Each flake is lit for an instant by the window's glow, and then it vanishes into the dark, and the next one takes its place. Beyond them, far across the valley, a few windows shine amber, in the white, like the last embers of a fire.

show.cap: Snow falling past a cottage window

segments.say: Snow has a special quiet. It lays itself on everything, on roofs, and branches, and fences, and fields, and it swallows the sounds of the world. The usual noises, the hum of roads, the clang of work, the bark of dogs, all of it softens, and then falls away, until there's only a deep, thick, cushioned silence.

Listen to that silence. It isn't empty. It's rich, and dense, like fresh wool. It wraps around your ears, and soothes them. It tells you that the world has stopped, for now, and that nothing is expected of you, and that you can stay here, in the warm, for as long as you like.

Behind you, there's a low fire, glowing in a stone hearth, throwing a warm light across the ceiling beams. It crackles very rarely, and very softly, like someone turning a page. Its warmth reaches you across the room, and settles over your back, and your shoulders, and the back of your neck.
Outside, the world is white and still. Inside, you are warm and safe.

show.text: Outside, the world is white and still. Inside, you are warm and safe.

segments.say: Watch the flakes for a while, and let your eyes follow one, from the top of the window to the bottom. It takes such a long time. It turns, and sways, and drifts, and never quite seems to arrive. And your eyelids, following it, grow heavier and heavier, until you can't quite remember if they're closed.

If the glass is cold enough, your breath might leave a small, soft mist on it, which grows, and fades, and grows again, with each slow breath. A little round cloud, appearing and disappearing, as steady as a sleeping pulse. You might watch it, and feel yourself drifting along with it.

A sleepy warmth spreads through you, starting at the top of your head, and flowing slowly down. Your forehead. Your eyes. Your cheeks and jaw. Your neck, your shoulders, and your arms. Your chest, your belly, your back. Your hips, your thighs, your knees, your calves, and your feet. All warm, all heavy, all soft.

And now, every part of you lets go, completely. No muscle holds on. No thought grips. Everything is released into the cushion, the blanket, the quiet, and the falling snow. It's the deepest kind of letting go, the kind that doesn't ask permission, and doesn't need to.

The snow will keep falling all night, soft and steady, covering the valley in a deep and gentle quilt. By morning, the world will be new. But that's for later. For now, there's only the window, and the flakes, and the warmth, and you, resting, resting, resting.
